prompt: What does a production possibility curve (PPC) show?

options.label: A
options.text: The combinations of goods consumers would most prefer, regardless of the productive resources and technology available.

options.label: B
options.text: Minimum combinations needed to employ every worker.

options.label: C
options.text: Maximum combinations attainable with given resources and technology.

options.label: D
options.text: Combinations sold at equal prices in product markets.

explanation: A PPC is a boundary of productive possibilities. It shows the maximum attainable combinations of two outputs when the available resources and technology are used fully and efficiently.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which assumption is made when a single PPC is drawn for an economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources and production technology are given.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer preferences cannot change over time.

options.label: C
options.text: Product prices remain constant across markets.

options.label: D
options.text: Production consists exclusively of public goods.

explanation: A PPC is drawn for a given productive capacity. That capacity depends on the quantity and quality of resources and on technology; changes in those determinants shift the curve.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economy is producing at a point on its PPC. What does this show?

options.label: A
options.text: It achieves a maximum attainable output combination.

options.label: B
options.text: It has eliminated the scarcity of resources.

options.label: C
options.text: It necessarily maximises consumers' welfare from consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: It can increase both outputs with existing resources.

explanation: A point on the PPC is attainable and productively efficient given current resources and technology. The diagram alone does not show that the combination is socially preferred.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A point lies outside an economy's current PPC. What does this mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The combination is currently beyond productive capacity.

options.label: B
options.text: The combination is attainable through higher unemployment.

options.label: C
options.text: The combination demonstrates inefficient use of existing capacity.

options.label: D
options.text: The combination is attainable without sacrificing other output.

explanation: A point outside the frontier is beyond current productive capacity. It may become attainable after productive capacity expands, but it is not attainable under the conditions represented by the current PPC.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A point lies inside an economy's PPC. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy must be allocating all resources to one good and cannot produce any quantity of the other.

options.label: B
options.text: Some resources are unemployed or are being used inefficiently.

options.label: C
options.text: All resources are fully and efficiently employed.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy has exceeded its productive capacity.

explanation: An interior point is attainable but inefficient: the economy could produce more of at least one good without reducing the other by making fuller or better use of existing resources.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why is a straight-line PPC associated with constant opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: Extra output requires no sacrifice of the other good.

options.label: B
options.text: Each extra unit requires the same output sacrifice.

options.label: C
options.text: Extra output requires progressively larger sacrifices of the other good.

options.label: D
options.text: Each extra unit requires a smaller output sacrifice.

explanation: A straight line has a constant slope. This means the quantity of one good sacrificed for each additional unit of the other is unchanged along the frontier.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why is a PPC usually bowed out from the origin?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers' preferences become increasingly balanced between the two goods.

options.label: B
options.text: Resources differ in their suitability for the two goods.

options.label: C
options.text: Both goods have progressively lower prices as output increases.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources become equally adaptable between the two productive industries.

explanation: With specialised resources, the resources transferred first are relatively well suited to the expanding activity. Further expansion requires resources increasingly well suited to the sacrificed activity, so marginal opportunity cost rises.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to shift an economy's PPC outwards?

options.label: A
options.text: A reallocation of existing workers between the two industries.

options.label: B
options.text: A change in consumer tastes from one good to another.

options.label: C
options.text: An improvement in production technology used throughout the economy.

options.label: D
options.text: A rise in unemployment with resources unchanged.

explanation: A general technological improvement raises the maximum output possible from given resources, increasing productive capacity and shifting the PPC outwards.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which change is most likely to shift an economy's PPC inwards?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployed workers find jobs using existing factories.

options.label: B
options.text: A major earthquake destroys part of the economy's capital stock.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers decide to purchase a wider range of services instead of goods, without any loss of productive resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Workers move from agriculture to manufacturing.

explanation: Destruction of physical capital reduces the quantity of productive resources available, lowering maximum possible output and shifting the PPC inwards.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country has high unemployment but its quantity and quality of resources are unchanged. What happens to its PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Capacity falls and the frontier shifts inwards.

options.label: B
options.text: Capacity rises and the frontier shifts outwards.

options.label: C
options.text: Capacity remains unchanged but unemployment makes the opportunity cost constant and therefore straightens the production frontier.

options.label: D
options.text: Capacity is unchanged but output may lie inside.

explanation: Unemployment reduces actual use of resources, not the economy's productive capacity itself. With resources and technology unchanged, the PPC stays in the same position while production can move inside it.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government moves workers and machinery from producing consumer goods to producing capital goods, with resources and technology unchanged. What does this cause?

options.label: A
options.text: A movement along the existing PPC.

options.label: B
options.text: A movement from outside the PPC to inside it.

options.label: C
options.text: An outward shift of the whole PPC.

options.label: D
options.text: An inward shift of the whole PPC.

explanation: Reallocating existing resources between the two outputs changes the combination produced but not productive capacity. It is represented by a movement along the existing frontier.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A technological improvement affects only the production of agricultural goods. What is the most likely effect on a PPC with agricultural goods on the vertical axis?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: The vertical intercept moves outward while the horizontal intercept is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: The curve is unchanged because technology affects only one good.

explanation: Sector-specific technology raises only the maximum output of the affected good. The PPC therefore pivots outward on the agricultural-goods axis rather than shifting uniformly.

prompt: A rise in the working-age population increases the labour available to all industries. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy necessarily moves to a point outside its PPC.

options.label: B
options.text: The PPC shifts inwards because average output per worker must fall.

options.label: C
options.text: The PPC shifts outwards because productive capacity increases.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy moves along an unchanged PPC.

explanation: More available labour increases the quantity of a factor of production. Other things equal, the economy can produce larger maximum combinations, so its PPC shifts outwards.

prompt: Which event would change the position of production without shifting the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: A reduction in unemployment using the existing stock of resources.

options.label: B
options.text: A permanent loss of fertile land.

options.label: C
options.text: An improvement in worker skills across industries.

options.label: D
options.text: Introducing a production technique that permanently raises the output each employed worker can produce with the same resources.

explanation: Bringing idle resources back into use moves the production point toward the frontier. The other changes alter productive capacity and therefore shift the PPC.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A straight-line PPC has the equation Y = 240 - 2X. What is the opportunity cost of one extra unit of X?

options.label: A
options.text: 120 units of Y.

options.label: B
options.text: 2 units of Y.

options.label: C
options.text: 0.5 units of Y.

options.label: D
options.text: 240 units of Y.

explanation: The coefficient of X is -2. Along the frontier, increasing X by one unit requires Y to fall by two units, so the opportunity cost of one X is two units of Y.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What will always increase when an economy's PPC shifts outwards?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of workers currently employed in producing the two goods.

options.label: B
options.text: Its exports.

options.label: C
options.text: Its current output.

options.label: D
options.text: Its productive capacity.

explanation: An outward PPC shift means the maximum output combinations the economy can produce have increased. Current output, employment and exports need not rise automatically.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which point on a PPC diagram represents productive inefficiency?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: A point inside the PPC.

options.label: C
options.text: Any point on the PPC.

options.label: D
options.text: A point beyond the PPC.

explanation: An interior point indicates that the economy is not obtaining the maximum output possible from its current resources and technology.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economy moves from a point inside its PPC to a point on the PPC while producing the same quantity of good Y. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: Productive capacity must rise as output expands.

options.label: B
options.text: The economy's frontier must shift outwards.

options.label: C
options.text: X can increase without sacrificing any Y.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy's productive resources must fall.

explanation: Starting inside the frontier means there is spare capacity or inefficiency. Better utilisation can raise X while leaving Y unchanged until the frontier is reached.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

explanation: Because the lost resource is specific to crop production, maximum crop output falls while maximum service output is unaffected. The PPC pivots inward on the crop axis.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Training permanently improves workers' productivity across the economy.

options.label: C
options.text: Exploration discovers additional commercially usable mineral reserves.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower cyclical unemployment brings existing idle resources into use.

prompt: What does the slope of a PPC measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment relative to the available labour force.

options.label: B
options.text: The ratio between the market prices consumers currently pay for the two products.

options.label: C
options.text: The output sacrificed for additional units of a good.

options.label: D
options.text: Technological progress relative to the initial production method.

explanation: The slope shows how much of one output must be sacrificed to obtain an additional amount of the other while remaining on the production frontier.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country improves the education and training of its workforce. Other things equal, what is the likely effect on its PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Unchanged frontier because the labour force size is fixed.

options.label: B
options.text: Vertical frontier because labour becomes completely specialised.

options.label: C
options.text: Inward shift because training reduces productive labour quality.

options.label: D
options.text: Outward shift because training improves productive labour quality.

explanation: Education and training can increase human capital and worker productivity. This raises the quality of a productive resource and therefore the economy's productive capacity.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement about an outward shift of a PPC is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Some previously unattainable combinations may become attainable.

options.label: B
options.text: All previously inefficient combinations must immediately become efficient.

options.label: C
options.text: The scarcity of productive resources must disappear entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual output must immediately reach the new frontier.

explanation: An outward shift expands the set of attainable combinations. It increases capacity, but the economy may still operate inside the new frontier and scarcity remains.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A combination of goods is attainable and productively efficient. Where must it lie?

options.label: A
options.text: Outside the PPC.

options.label: B
options.text: Inside the PPC.

options.label: C
options.text: At the origin only.

options.label: D
options.text: On the PPC.

explanation: Points on the frontier are the maximum combinations attainable from current resources and technology, so they are attainable and productively efficient.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which change will not by itself shift a PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: A change in consumers' preferences between the two goods.

options.label: B
options.text: A change in production technology.

options.label: C
options.text: A change in the quantity of labour.

options.label: D
options.text: A change in the quality of capital.

explanation: Preferences can alter which point on the frontier is chosen, but they do not alter the maximum quantities the economy is capable of producing.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

options.label: C
options.text: Production moves beyond the frontier towards consumer goods.

options.label: D
options.text: The frontier shifts inwards towards both production axes.

explanation: With productive capacity unchanged and resources fully employed, changing the output mix requires reallocation between the two goods and therefore a movement along the PPC.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government increases investment in capital goods by reallocating resources away from consumer goods. What is the immediate PPC effect and a possible later effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate movement outside; later a return to the original frontier.

options.label: B
options.text: An immediate outward shift because reallocation alone creates extra resources; later, movement inside the original frontier as capital accumulates.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate inward shift; later unchanged capacity for both goods.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate movement along; possible later outward shift from capital accumulation.

explanation: The initial choice changes the current output mix and is therefore a movement along the PPC. Additional capital can subsequently increase the economy's resource stock and shift future production possibilities outward.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country produces less capital than the amount required to replace worn-out machinery. Other things equal, what is the likely long-run effect on its PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: It shifts inward as the capital stock declines.

options.label: B
options.text: It shifts outward because current consumption is higher.

options.label: C
options.text: It becomes a straight line because opportunity cost is constant.

options.label: D
options.text: It remains fixed because depreciation affects only actual output.

explanation: If investment is insufficient to replace depreciated capital, the stock of productive capital falls. This reduces productive capacity and can shift the PPC inward.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country launches a successful economy-wide training programme that raises output per worker, but at the same time unemployment rises because aggregate demand falls. What is the most likely combination?

options.label: A
options.text: Capacity rises while output may move further inside the frontier.

options.label: B
options.text: Capacity is unchanged because unemployment offsets the training improvement.

options.label: C
options.text: Output exceeds the new frontier because workers are more productive.

options.label: D

prompt: An economy has an initial straight-line PPC from 90 Y to 90 X. After a sector-specific innovation, the X-intercept rises to 180 while the Y-intercept remains 90. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of an extra unit of Y falls from 0.5 units of X to 1 unit of X.

options.label: B
options.text: The opportunity cost of X doubles.

options.label: C
options.text: The PPC shifts inward because its slope becomes flatter.

options.label: D
options.text: The opportunity cost of one X falls from 1 Y to 0.5 Y.

explanation: Initially the trade-off is 90 Y for 90 X, or 1 Y per X. Afterwards it is 90 Y for 180 X, or 0.5 Y per X. The X-specific innovation lowers X's opportunity cost.

prompt: Which statement is not necessarily true of a point inside a PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Output falls below the economy's maximum attainable combinations.

options.label: B
options.text: At least one output may rise without reducing the other.

options.label: C
options.text: Some productive capacity is unused or inefficiently employed.

options.label: D
options.text: Some workers necessarily have no employment at this combination.

explanation: An interior point indicates underutilisation or inefficiency, but the problem need not specifically be unemployment of labour. Capital or land may be idle, or resources may simply be used inefficiently.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An economy is at point A on its PPC. It then experiences an outward shift but continues to produce at exactly A. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A becomes inefficient relative to the expanded productive frontier.

options.label: B
options.text: A necessarily remains efficient on the expanded productive frontier.

options.label: C
options.text: Actual output necessarily rises to the expanded productive frontier.

options.label: D
options.text: A becomes unattainable despite the expansion of productive capacity.

explanation: Once the frontier shifts outward, the unchanged output combination A lies inside the new PPC. It is still attainable, but no longer represents full use of the economy's expanded productive capacity.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government subsidises demand for good X, causing firms to reallocate resources toward X. The amount and quality of resources and technology are unchanged. Which diagrammatic change is appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: The frontier contracts towards the origin in both directions.

options.label: B
options.text: The frontier expands outwards in parallel in both directions.

options.label: C
options.text: The frontier pivots outwards along the horizontal axis because stronger consumer demand automatically increases the maximum attainable X output.

options.label: D
options.text: Output moves along the frontier towards more X and less Y.

explanation: A demand-side change can alter the output mix but does not itself alter the economy's production possibilities. With full employment it is represented by a movement along the existing frontier.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A sector-specific technological advance raises the maximum output of X. At the same time, a drought reduces the maximum output of Y. What is the most likely graphical result?

options.label: A
options.text: The new PPC must lie wholly outside the old PPC.

options.label: B
options.text: The new PPC must lie wholly inside the old PPC.

options.label: C
options.text: The new PPC may cross the old PPC.

options.label: D
options.text: The PPC must remain unchanged because the effects offset.

explanation: Capacity has improved in one activity and deteriorated in the other. A new frontier with a larger X-intercept and smaller Y-intercept can therefore cross the original PPC.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country can initially produce either 100 capital goods or 400 consumer goods on a straight-line PPC. After investment, the maximum capital output rises to 125 and maximum consumer output to 500. What happens to the opportunity cost of one capital good?

options.label: A
options.text: It rises from 4 to 5 consumer goods.

options.label: B
options.text: It remains 4 consumer goods.

options.label: C
options.text: It becomes 0.25 consumer goods.

options.label: D
options.text: It falls from 4 to 3 consumer goods.

explanation: Initially one capital good costs 400/100 = 4 consumer goods. Afterwards it costs 500/125 = 4. The frontier expands proportionately, so the slope and constant opportunity cost are unchanged.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt:
The schedule below changes after a technological improvement. Which industry most clearly receives the larger productivity gain?
| Output limit | Before | After |
| Maximum X | 60 | 90 |
| Maximum Y | 120 | 132 |

options.label: A
options.text: The table cannot indicate any sectoral difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Both industries receive exactly the same gain.

options.label: C
options.text: Industry X.

options.label: D
options.text: Industry Y.

explanation: The maximum X intercept rises from 60 to 90, a 50% increase, while the maximum Y intercept rises from 120 to 132, a 10% increase. Productive capacity expands much more in X.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economy's PPC is bowed out. A policy raises the mobility of resources between the two industries without increasing the quantity or quality of resources. What could happen to the shape of the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: The frontier must expand outwards at every possible combination.

options.label: B
options.text: The frontier must contract because resources become less specialised.

options.label: C
options.text: The frontier could become less bowed as transfer costs fall.

options.label: D
options.text: The frontier must become vertical because only one good remains.

explanation: Greater factor mobility can make resources more adaptable between uses. This can reduce the rise in marginal opportunity cost associated with reallocation, changing curvature even without a simple uniform capacity increase.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a shift of a PPC from a movement along it?

options.label: A
options.text: Shifts indicate unemployment; movements indicate full employment.

options.label: B
options.text: Shifts change attainable combinations; movements reallocate within unchanged capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Shifts increase both outputs; movements necessarily reduce both outputs.

options.label: D
options.text: Shifts reflect demand changes; movements reflect technological progress.

explanation: A movement along the frontier is reallocation with productive capacity fixed. A shift changes productive capacity itself and therefore changes the boundary of attainable combinations.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.1 nature and meaning of a production possibility curve (PPC) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: The economy moves from A to B on a bowed-out PPC and then from B to C after an outward shift. Why is it invalid to calculate the opportunity cost of B to C simply as the output sacrificed along the old PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Old frontier points were inefficient before capacity increased.

options.label: B
options.text: Opportunity cost cannot apply when both outputs increase.

options.label: C
options.text: Opportunity cost can apply only to linear production frontiers.

options.label: D
options.text: The change is not a reallocation along unchanged capacity.

explanation: Opportunity cost shown by the slope of a PPC concerns movements along a given frontier. A shift changes the production possibilities themselves, so the simple along-curve trade-off does not describe B to C.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country uses previously unemployed resources and at the same time adopts a new technology. Which outcome is possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Capacity can rise but actual output cannot change.

options.label: B
options.text: Actual output must move beyond the expanded productive frontier.

options.label: C
options.text: Capacity cannot rise while unused resources enter productive use.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual output can rise while productive capacity also expands.

explanation: The two events affect different dimensions: greater utilisation changes actual production relative to capacity, while technology expands productive capacity. Both can occur simultaneously.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country can produce either 50 units of X or 100 units of Y with a straight-line PPC. A new process raises the X maximum to 100 but leaves Y unchanged. If it produces 40 X after the change, what is the maximum Y?

options.label: A
options.text: 20 units.

options.label: B
options.text: 40 units.

options.label: C
options.text: 80 units.

options.label: D
options.text: 60 units.

explanation: After the improvement, one X costs 100/100 = 1 Y. Producing 40 X therefore sacrifices 40 Y from the maximum 100, leaving 60 Y.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which conclusion is valid if a PPC shifts outward but becomes more bowed?

options.label: A
options.text: Opportunity costs become identical for all attainable output combinations.

options.label: B
options.text: Capacity expands while marginal opportunity costs change more sharply.

options.label: C
options.text: Scarcity disappears because the economy's maximum potential production rises.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual output rises in exactly the same proportion as capacity.

explanation: Position and curvature convey different information. An outward shift concerns capacity; greater curvature concerns how opportunity cost changes as resources are reallocated.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country is producing on its PPC at A. It experiences a recession and moves to B inside the PPC. Later, without any change in resources or technology, it returns to A. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Capacity remains unchanged while utilisation falls and then recovers.

options.label: B
options.text: Capacity necessarily falls permanently as soon as recession begins.

options.label: C
options.text: Productive capacity necessarily contracts when unemployment rises, then expands again when the same resources return to employment.

options.label: D
options.text: The original combination becomes unattainable during the economic recession.

explanation: A recession can move actual production inside a given frontier because resources are underused. If resources and technology are unchanged, recovery can return output to the original frontier without a PPC shift.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
The table shows four output combinations. The current PPC passes through A, B and C. D lies outside it. After a technological change, D becomes attainable while A, B and C remain attainable. What must have happened?
| Combination | X | Y |
| A | 0 | 100 |
| B | 30 | 85 |
| C | 60 | 50 |
| D | 70 | 70 |

options.label: A
options.text: The set of production possibilities expanded.

options.label: B
options.text: The opportunity cost of both goods became zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy necessarily chose D as its actual output.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy moved along an unchanged PPC.

explanation: If a previously unattainable combination becomes attainable without losing the old attainable combinations, productive capacity has expanded. This is represented by an outward change in the frontier.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economy is producing at a point on its PPC. Which conclusion is not justified by this information alone?

options.label: A
options.text: The output combination is attainable with current resources and technology.

options.label: B
options.text: Productive capacity is being fully used for the two outputs shown.

options.label: C
options.text: The chosen combination is the one that maximises society's welfare.

options.label: D
options.text: Producing more of one good on the existing frontier would require sacrificing some of the other.

explanation: A point on the PPC shows an attainable, productively efficient output combination. It does not contain information about society's preferences or welfare, so the diagram alone cannot establish that the chosen combination is socially optimal.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country's working population falls by 10%, but average productivity rises by 10%. If labour is the only changing determinant and the effects are multiplicative, what happens to maximum output?

options.label: A
options.text: It falls by 1%.

options.label: B
options.text: It falls by 10%.

options.label: C
options.text: It rises by 1%.

options.label: D
options.text: It is unchanged.

explanation: Maximum output is proportional to labour times productivity. 0.90 x 1.10 = 0.99, so productive capacity is 99% of its former level, a 1% fall.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economy has an interior point P and a frontier point Q directly above it, with the same X output. What is the opportunity cost of moving from P to Q in terms of X?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal to the frontier's slope at point Q.

options.label: B
options.text: Zero X, since the move leaves X unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal to the whole increase in Y output.

options.label: D
options.text: Positive X, since every increase requires a sacrifice.

explanation: When moving from an inefficient interior point toward the frontier, extra output can be obtained by using idle or inefficiently used resources. If X is unchanged, the measured sacrifice of X is zero for that move.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.4 significance of a position within a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A new technology raises the maximum possible output of both goods, but it raises X proportionately more than Y. Which combination of effects is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Capacity contracts because the relative productivity of resources changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Output moves along the frontier without any change in capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Capacity expands equally in both directions with unchanged opportunity costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Capacity expands with a change in relative production possibilities.

explanation: Productive capacity expands in both sectors, but asymmetrically. The frontier therefore moves outward while its shape or slope relative to the axes can also change.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is most defensible about the opportunity cost shown by a PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: It depends exclusively on intercepts rather than frontier movements.

options.label: B
options.text: It necessarily equals the ratio of the two market prices.

options.label: C
options.text: It disappears when resources are fully employed on the frontier.

options.label: D
options.text: It measures an output trade-off rather than necessarily money costs.

explanation: The PPC measures opportunity cost in physical units of alternative output forgone. Market prices can differ from this physical production trade-off.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.2 shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country moves resources from consumer goods to capital goods today. Under what condition is an outward PPC shift in the future most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Households keep their initial preferences between the two goods.

options.label: B
options.text: Firms keep output at the maximum consumer-goods combination.

options.label: C
options.text: Market prices of capital goods rise relative to consumer goods.

options.label: D
options.text: Additional capital exceeds depreciation and expands future productive capacity.

explanation: Producing capital goods can support future growth only if net additions to the productive capital stock occur. If new capital merely replaces depreciation, productive capacity may be maintained rather than expanded.
reference: 1.5 Production possibility curves | 1.5.3 causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC | AO3 Evaluation
